content.title: What is MLB’s ABS Challenge System? How Ball-Strike Challenges Work During Games | Sportsnet Pittsburgh
content.text: If you are watching a baseball game and see a hitter, catcher or pitcher tap their helmet right after a close pitch, you are looking at MLB’s ABS challenge system.ABS stands for Automated Ball-Strike system, but the version used in the majors is not full-time “robot umpiring.” The home-plate umpire still makes every call live, and the technology only steps in when a player challenges a ball-or-strike decision.MLB rolled the system out for the 2026 season after testing it in the minors and in Major League spring training.What the ABS challenge system actually does Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn ImagesThe easiest way to think about ABS is that it works like a limited review tool for the strike zone. The umpire makes the original call. If the pitcher, catcher or batter thinks the call was wrong, that player can challenge it immediately. The system then checks the tracked pitch location against the hitter’s strike zone and either confirms or overturns the call, with the result shown quickly on the ballpark videoboard and on the TV broadcast.That is why ABS is different from the old robot umpire idea people used to debate. MLB did not remove the human plate umpire. It kept the human call as the default and added a fast correction system for the moments players feel matter most.Who can challenge, and when?This is the part most fans want answered right away during a game.Only the batter, pitcher or catcher can challenge a pitch. Managers, coaches and other fielders cannot.The challenge has to be made immediately after the call, generally within about two seconds.The player signals it by tapping his helmet or cap, usually while also saying something to the umpire.If a challenge is made too late, or if the umpire thinks the dugout or other players helped decide it, the umpire can disallow the request.That timing matters. MLB wants the challenge to come from the player’s own feel in the moment, not from a delayed signal after someone in the dugout sees a replay. So when you see a player react instantly, that is by design.How many challenges teams get Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn ImagesEach team starts a game with two challenges. If a team wins a challenge, it keeps it. If the umpire’s original call is confirmed, that challenge is gone. That setup is a big reason the system adds some strategy instead of turning every borderline pitch into a review. Players have to decide whether a close call is worth spending one of the team’s limited chances.Extra innings work a little differently. If a team begins an extra inning with no challenges left, it receives one for that inning. If it still has a challenge remaining, it does not get an extra one just for reaching extras.There are also a couple of limits fans should know:Challenges are not allowed when a position player is pitching.Challenges are also not permitted after replay reviews, to avoid stacking one review process on top of another.How the strike zone is judgedThe technology is checking the pitch against a strike zone that is standardized, but also personalized to each batter. MLB says the zone is a two-dimensional plane measured at the middle of home plate, not the front edge. It is 17 inches wide, matching the width of the plate. The top of the zone is set at 53.5% of the hitter’s height without cleats, and the bottom is set at 27% of that height. If any part of the baseball touches any part of that zone, it is a strike.That detail explains why some challenge results may look a little different from the TV strike-zone box fans are used to. The broadcast box is just a graphic. ABS is using Hawk-Eye tracking and a measured zone tied to the specific hitter. MLB says 12 cameras track the pitch, with accuracy measured down to around one-sixth of an inch.Does ABS slow the game down?Not much. In MLB’s 2025 spring training test, there were 4.1 challenges per game on average, and each one took 13.8 seconds. That works out to under a minute of added time per game on average. MLB also said pitches per plate appearance stayed basically unchanged during testing, so the challenge system did not create a bunch of longer at-bats.The best way to think about ABS, then, is simple: it is not there to re-call every pitch. It is there to give players a limited chance to correct the biggest misses without taking the umpire out of the game. So the next time you see that quick helmet tap, you are watching baseball’s new way of saying, Let’s check it.
